title: Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Defining a Competitive Market
questions.prompt_template: Which institutional characteristic defines a competitive market in the Chapter 3 supply-and-demand model?

hints.text: Think about how much influence any individual buyer or seller has over the market price.
A competitive market has many buyers and sellers trading a standardized good so that everyone takes the market price as given.

options_template.text: A single dominant producer sets the list price while many small buyers choose how much to purchase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopoly Confusion): A market with one dominant price-setting producer is a monopoly, not a competitive market.

options_template.text: Many buyers and sellers trade a standardized good so that no single buyer or seller can dictate the market price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In a competitive market, numerous buyers and sellers exchange a standardized product, making each participant a price taker.

options_template.text: Government regulators establish fixed legal prices for every transaction so that prices never fluctuate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Administered-Price Fallacy): Competitive markets rely on flexible price discovery rather than universal government price fixing.

options_template.text: Buyers and sellers negotiate customized, one-of-a-kind contracts with completely differentiated goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Product Differentiation Confusion): The competitive benchmark assumes a standardized good rather than unique bespoke contracts.

questions.topic: Single-Market Price vs. Aggregate Price Level
questions.title: Distinguishing Single-Market Price from Aggregate Price Level
questions.prompt_template: In Chapter 3, how does the variable P differ from the aggregate price level studied later in macroeconomics?

hints.text: Compare the units and scope of a single product's price tag against an economy-wide index like the CPI.
In Chapter 3, P is the dollar price of one specific good (holding other prices constant), whereas the aggregate price level is a unitless index across a broad basket.

options_template.text: P is the nominal dollar price of a single good or service, whereas the aggregate price level is a unitless index measuring overall prices across a representative basket of goods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Chapter 3 analyzes single-market prices (such as dollars per bag of coffee), keeping them distinct from economy-wide price indexes covered in Chapter 5.

options_template.text: P is always adjusted for inflation using a base-year deflator, whereas the aggregate price level is measured in raw dollars per unit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Real-vs-Nominal Inversion): Single-market P in Chapter 3 is a nominal dollar price per unit, while the aggregate price level is a unitless index.

options_template.text: P represents the total revenue of all firms in the economy, whereas the aggregate price level measures only household wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate-Output Confusion): Neither P nor the aggregate price level measures total revenue or wages alone.

options_template.text: There is no conceptual difference; single-market supply and demand directly determine the economy-wide Consumer Price Index.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fallacy of Composition): A single product's price reflects relative scarcity in one market, not economy-wide inflation across all goods.

questions.title: Law of Demand and Ceteris Paribus
questions.prompt_template: What does the Law of Demand state, holding all other factors constant (ceteris paribus)?

hints.text: Focus on the direction of relationship between a good's own price and the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy.
The Law of Demand describes an inverse relationship between own price and quantity demanded.

options_template.text: When a good's own price rises, consumers' overall demand curve shifts rightward to preserve spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): A change in own price never shifts the demand curve; it causes a movement along a fixed curve.

options_template.text: When a good's own price rises, quantity demanded rises because higher prices signal superior quality.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Quality Fallacy): Under the Law of Demand, higher own prices reduce quantity demanded, ceteris paribus.

options_template.text: There is an inverse relationship between a good's own price and its quantity demanded: higher prices reduce quantity demanded and lower prices increase it.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Holding non-price determinants fixed, buyers purchase fewer units when own price rises and more units when own price falls.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded depends exclusively on household income and is unaffected by the good's own price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Price-Responsiveness Fallacy): Own price is the primary determinant of quantity demanded along a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.title: Why Demand Curves Slope Downward
questions.prompt_template: Which two behavioral mechanisms explain why a higher own price reduces quantity demanded along a downward-sloping demand curve?

hints.text: Consider both how a higher price changes a good's relative cost compared to alternatives and how it affects household purchasing power.
Economists decompose the downward slope of demand into the substitution effect and the income effect.

options_template.text: The diminishing marginal productivity effect and the fixed-capacity cost effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Attribution): Diminishing marginal productivity explains rising marginal cost and upward-sloping supply, not downward-sloping demand.

options_template.text: The menu-cost effect and the sticky-wage effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro-Rigidity Confusion): Menu costs and sticky wages relate to macroeconomic nominal rigidities, not individual consumer demand slopes.

options_template.text: The price-ceiling effect and the non-price rationing effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Intervention Confusion): Price ceilings and rationing arise from legal price caps, not from the underlying downward slope of demand.

options_template.text: The substitution effect (switching toward cheaper alternatives) and the income effect (lower purchasing power of fixed nominal income).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher own price makes substitutes relatively cheaper and erodes real purchasing power, both of which reduce quantity demanded.

questions.topic: Demand Shifters: Normal vs. Inferior Goods
questions.title: Distinguishing Normal Goods from Inferior Goods
questions.prompt_template: How does an increase in household income affect the demand curves for a normal good (such as restaurant dining) and an inferior good (such as instant noodles)?

hints.text: Ask whether households buy more or less of each item at the same price when their budgets expand.
Higher income shifts demand rightward for normal goods and leftward for inferior goods.

options_template.text: Demand shifts rightward for restaurant dining (normal good) and leftward for instant noodles (inferior good).
options_template.feedback: Correct. By definition, higher income increases demand at every price for normal goods and decreases demand at every price for inferior goods.

options_template.text: Demand shifts rightward for both goods because higher income always raises spending on every product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal Normal-Good Fallacy): Consumers substitute away from inferior goods as income rises, shifting inferior-good demand leftward.

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward for restaurant dining and rightward for instant noodles.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal-Inferior Inversion): This reverses the definitions of normal and inferior goods.

options_template.text: Neither demand curve shifts; instead, households move downward along both fixed demand curves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): Income is a non-price determinant, so a change in income shifts the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.

questions.title: Substitutes versus Complements
questions.prompt_template: Suppose tea is a substitute for coffee and espresso machines are a complement to coffee. How does a sharp price hike in each related good shift the demand curve for coffee?

hints.text: Think about how buyers react when an alternative good becomes more expensive versus when a jointly used good becomes more expensive.
A higher price for a substitute increases demand for the primary good; a higher price for a complement reduces demand for the primary good.

options_template.text: Higher tea prices shift coffee demand leftward; higher espresso-machine prices shift coffee demand rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Inversion): This reverses the directional effects of substitutes and complements.

options_template.text: Higher tea prices shift coffee demand rightward; higher espresso-machine prices shift coffee demand leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When tea gets pricier, buyers switch toward coffee (D shifts right); when espresso machines get pricier, fewer people brew espresso at home (coffee D shifts left).

options_template.text: Both price hikes shift coffee demand leftward because any higher price in the economy lowers coffee demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Negative-Cross-Effect Fallacy): Higher substitute prices actually increase demand for the primary good as buyers switch away from the pricier rival.

options_template.text: Neither price hike shifts coffee demand because only a change in the price of coffee itself affects coffee buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price Exclusivity Fallacy): Prices of related goods are a core non-price determinant that shifts the coffee demand curve.

questions.topic: Law of Supply and Marginal Opportunity Cost
questions.title: Why Short-Run Supply Curves Slope Upward
questions.prompt_template: Why do competitive supply curves slope upward from left to right in the short run?

hints.text: Consider what happens to per-unit incremental cost when firms expand output using fixed plant capacity and equipment.
Diminishing marginal productivity raises marginal opportunity cost as output grows, so firms require a higher price to supply additional units.

options_template.text: Because consumers are always willing to pay higher prices when firms produce larger quantities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Confusion): Consumer willingness to pay governs the downward-sloping demand curve, not the upward-sloping supply curve.

options_template.text: Because higher output lowers per-unit variable costs indefinitely, allowing firms to charge higher markups.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Marginal-Cost Fallacy): Falling marginal costs would not require a higher price to induce extra output; short-run supply slopes up due to rising marginal cost.

options_template.text: Because fixed short-run capacity creates diminishing marginal productivity and rising marginal opportunity cost, requiring higher prices to justify extra units.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expanding output with fixed plant and equipment requires more variable inputs per incremental unit, so firms only expand Qs when market price rises to cover higher marginal cost.

options_template.text: Because government excise taxes automatically increase whenever a firm sells more units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Driven Slope Fallacy): Supply curves slope upward due to rising marginal opportunity cost even in markets with zero excise taxes.

questions.title: Identifying Valid Supply Shifters
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following changes causes a shift of the entire market supply curve rather than a movement along it?

hints.text: Separate the good's own market price and buyer-side factors from underlying production conditions.
Only non-price production determinants—input prices, technology, taxes/subsidies, producer expectations, or number of sellers—shift the supply curve.

options_template.text: An increase in the good's own market price caused by higher consumer demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a fixed supply curve (a change in quantity supplied).

options_template.text: A favorable shift in consumer tastes toward the product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-vs-Supply Shifter Confusion): Consumer tastes shift the demand curve, which then induces a movement along the fixed supply curve.

options_template.text: An increase in the number of buyers entering the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Size Side Confusion): More buyers shift the demand curve rightward; it is the number of active producers that shifts supply.

options_template.text: A decline in raw material and energy prices used by producers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lower input prices reduce marginal production cost at every output level, shifting the entire supply curve rightward.

questions.title: Meaning of Market-Clearing Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: What condition defines market equilibrium (P*, Q*) in a competitive single-product market?

hints.text: Compare the quantity buyers want to purchase and the quantity sellers want to offer at the prevailing price.
Equilibrium occurs at the unique price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, leaving no surplus or shortage.

options_template.text: At price P*, quantity demanded exactly equals quantity supplied (Qd = Qs = Q*), so buyer and seller plans are mutually compatible with no surplus or shortage.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Market-clearing equilibrium occurs where the demand and supply curves intersect, eliminating excess supply and excess demand.

options_template.text: At price P*, every consumer who wants the good receives it for free and firms earn zero revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Price Equilibrium Fallacy): Equilibrium requires Qd = Qs at a positive market-clearing price P*, not a zero price.

options_template.text: At price P*, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by a small buffer so stores always hold unsold inventory.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Permanent-Surplus Fallacy): Excess supply (Qs > Qd) is a disequilibrium surplus that puts downward pressure on price.

options_template.text: At price P*, the demand curve and supply curve have identical slopes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Equality Confusion): Equilibrium requires equality of quantities at P*, not equal slopes (demand slopes down while supply slopes up).

questions.title: Automatic Price-Discovery Forces in Disequilibrium
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market without price controls, what happens when the prevailing market price is temporarily below the equilibrium price P*?

hints.text: Compare Qd and Qs when price sits below the intersection of demand and supply.
Below P*, Qd exceeds Qs (a shortage), prompting frustrated buyers to bid prices up until the shortage clears.

options_template.text: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a surplus), causing sellers to cut prices toward P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Above-vs-Below Inversion): A surplus occurs when price is above P*, not below P*.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage), causing buyers to bid prices upward and sellers to raise quotes until price reaches P*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P < P*, excess demand drives price upward, contracting Qd and expanding Qs until the market clears at P*.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage), causing the demand curve to shift leftward automatically until P becomes the new equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous-Shift Fallacy): Price adjustment causes movements along fixed demand and supply curves rather than shifting the curves.

options_template.text: The market remains permanently stuck at the lower price because sellers never raise prices once listed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Price Fallacy): In a flexible competitive market, excess demand creates upward price pressure that eliminates the shortage.

questions.title: Defining a Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: When is a government-mandated price ceiling legally binding, and what market imbalance does it create?

hints.text: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. Ask whether a cap above or below P* actually stops the price from reaching equilibrium.
A ceiling binds only when set below P* (Pc < P*), blocking price from rising to clear excess demand.

options_template.text: It is binding when set above P* (Pc > P*), creating a persistent surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-Floor Inversion): A ceiling above P* is non-binding; a binding price floor is set above P* and creates a surplus.

options_template.text: It is binding when set above P* (Pc > P*), creating a persistent shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Binding Misclassification): If the legal maximum exceeds P*, the market legally clears at P* with no shortage.

options_template.text: It is binding when set below P* (Pc < P*), creating a persistent shortage because Qd(Pc) > Qs(Pc).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A binding price ceiling caps price below equilibrium, preventing upward price adjustment and sustaining excess demand.

options_template.text: It is binding at any level, and it always increases the total quantity bought and sold in the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expanded-Volume Fallacy): A binding ceiling reduces quantity supplied, so actual quantity traded falls below Q*.

questions.title: Defining a Binding Price Floor
questions.prompt_template: When is a government-mandated price floor legally binding, and what market outcome does it produce?

hints.text: A price floor is a legal minimum price. Determine whether a minimum set above or below P* prevents the market from clearing.
A floor binds only when set above P* (Pf > P*), keeping price from falling to eliminate excess supply.

options_template.text: It is binding when set below P* (Pf < P*), creating a persistent shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-Floor Inversion): A legal minimum set below P* is non-binding because the equilibrium price already satisfies the minimum.

options_template.text: It is binding when set below P* (Pf < P*), creating a persistent surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Binding Misclassification): When Pf < P*, the market legally clears at P* with zero surplus.

options_template.text: It is binding when set above P* (Pf > P*), creating a persistent shortage because buyers demand more at the higher guaranteed price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law-of-Demand Violation): Raising price above P* reduces quantity demanded and raises quantity supplied, producing a surplus rather than a shortage.

options_template.text: It is binding when set above P* (Pf > P*), creating a persistent surplus because Qs(Pf) > Qd(Pf).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A binding price floor holds price above equilibrium, discouraging buyers and inducing excess supply.

questions.title: Determining Actual Quantity Traded Under Regulated Prices
questions.prompt_template: At any regulated price P_bar where quantity demanded differs from quantity supplied, what determines the actual quantity exchanged in a voluntary market?

hints.text: Can sellers force buyers to purchase more than Qd, or can buyers force sellers to produce more than Qs?
Voluntary exchange requires both a willing buyer and a willing seller, so actual trades are limited by the smaller of Qd and Qs.

options_template.text: The short side of the market: Q_traded = min{Qd(P_bar), Qs(P_bar)}.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under a binding ceiling, trades are capped by Qs(Pc); under a binding floor, trades are capped by Qd(Pf).

options_template.text: The long side of the market: Q_traded = max{Qd(P_bar), Qs(P_bar)}.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Side Fallacy): Market trades cannot exceed what the constrained side is willing to buy or sell.

options_template.text: The arithmetic average of quantity demanded and quantity supplied: Q_traded = [Qd(P_bar) + Qs(P_bar)] / 2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint Averaging Fallacy): Averaging Qd and Qs overstates actual trades because no voluntary counterparty exists beyond the short side.

options_template.text: The original unregulated equilibrium quantity Q*, regardless of how far P_bar deviates from P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Invariance Fallacy): Any binding price ceiling or price floor reduces actual quantity traded strictly below Q*.

questions.title: Reading Movements Along vs. Shifts on a Demand Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In a specialty coffee market (Figure 3.1), initial demand D1 passes through Point A (Q = 200, P = $20) and Point B (Q = 300, P = $15), while a shifted curve D2 passes through Point C (Q = 300, P = $20). How are the transitions A -> B and A -> C classified?

hints.text: Check whether price changed or stayed constant in each transition.
A -> B changes price along the same curve D1; A -> C raises quantity at the unchanged price of $20 by moving onto D2.

options_template.text: A -> B is a rightward shift of demand, and A -> C is a movement along the demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-Shift Reversal): Changing own price ($20 to $15) is a movement along D1, whereas changing quantity at a fixed $20 price is a curve shift.

options_template.text: A -> B is an increase in quantity demanded (movement along D1), and A -> C is an increase in demand (rightward shift from D1 to D2).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lowering own price moves buyers along D1 from A to B, whereas a non-price determinant (such as higher income) shifts the entire curve right from A to C.

options_template.text: Both A -> B and A -> C represent rightward shifts of the demand curve because quantity increases by 100 units in both cases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Only Fallacy): Equal quantity increases (+100) do not imply the same graphical event; you must check whether own price changed.

options_template.text: Both A -> B and A -> C represent movements along D1 because Point B and Point C share the same quantity of 300 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shared-Quantity Confusion): Point C lies off D1 on a new demand schedule D2, so moving from A to C is a curve shift.

questions.title: Avoiding the Own-Price Shift Fallacy
questions.prompt_template: When a video-streaming platform raises its ad-free monthly subscription price from $15 to $20 and loses subscribers as a result, how should this change be depicted on the platform's demand graph?

hints.text: Ask whether the trigger is the platform's own price or a non-price determinant.
An own-price increase never shifts the demand curve; it moves the outcome upward and to the left along the existing demand curve.

options_template.text: As a leftward shift of the entire demand curve because fewer households subscribe.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price Shift Fallacy): Higher own price reduces quantity demanded via a movement along D, never a leftward shift of D.

options_template.text: As a rightward shift of the demand curve because the platform charges a higher price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Height Shift Confusion): Higher own price is read vertically along the existing curve, not as an outward shift.

options_template.text: As an upward and leftward movement along the fixed demand curve, representing a decrease in quantity demanded.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Holding non-price factors constant, raising own price from $15 to $20 moves buyers upward along the fixed demand curve.

options_template.text: As a vertical shift of the supply curve with no change on the demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Side-of-Market Confusion): Subscriber responses to a higher subscription fee are traced along the demand curve.

questions.title: Reading Movements Along vs. Shifts on a Supply Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In the roasted coffee supply diagram (Figure 3.2), curve S1 passes through A (Q = 200, P = $14) and B (Q = 300, P = $19), while curve S2 passes through C (Q = 260, P = $14). Which event moves the market from A to C rather than from A to B?

hints.text: Notice that at Point C, roasters supply 60 more bags at the exact same $14 price.
Moving from A to C is a rightward shift of supply caused by a non-price cost reduction, not a higher coffee price.

options_template.text: Lower import tariffs on raw green coffee beans reduce marginal roasting costs by $3 per bag, shifting supply rightward from S1 to S2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lower input costs shift the entire supply curve rightward, expanding quantity supplied from 200 to 260 bags at the unchanged $14 price.

options_template.text: The retail price of roasted coffee rises from $14 to $19 per bag, encouraging roasters to expand output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): A rise in own price from $14 to $19 moves roasters along S1 from A to B, not to C.

options_template.text: Higher household incomes increase consumer demand for specialty coffee.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shock Attribution): Higher consumer income shifts demand rightward and induces a movement upward along S1 rather than shifting S1 to S2.

options_template.text: A new per-unit excise tax is levied on coffee roasters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Direction Inversion): A per-unit excise tax raises marginal cost and shifts supply leftward, not rightward to S2.

questions.title: Interpreting Vertical Intercepts on a Price-Quantity Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a standard supply-and-demand diagram with Price (P) on the vertical axis and Quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis, what do the vertical intercepts of the linear demand curve and linear supply curve represent?

hints.text: Set Q = 0 in both inverse demand P = a/b - (1/b)Q and inverse supply P = -c/d + (1/d)Q.
At Q = 0, the demand vertical intercept is the choke price and the supply vertical intercept is the minimum reservation price.

options_template.text: The demand vertical intercept is maximum quantity demanded when P = 0, and the supply vertical intercept is the equilibrium quantity Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Intercept Swap): Maximum quantity demanded at P = 0 is the horizontal intercept of demand, not the vertical intercept.

options_template.text: Both vertical intercepts measure the slope of their respective curves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-Slope Confusion): Vertical intercepts are dollar prices at Q = 0, whereas slopes measure dP/dQ.

options_template.text: The demand vertical intercept is the shutdown reservation price, and the supply vertical intercept is the choke price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Choke-Reservation Inversion): The choke price belongs to demand (highest price where Qd hits 0) and the reservation price belongs to supply.

options_template.text: The demand vertical intercept is the choke price (price at which Qd = 0), and the supply vertical intercept is the shutdown reservation price (minimum price required for Qs > 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting Q = 0 gives the choke price a/b on inverse demand and the reservation price -c/d on inverse supply.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Rightward Demand Shift
questions.prompt_template: Starting from competitive equilibrium E1(Q*, P*), suppose a favorable health report shifts the demand curve for blueberries rightward while the supply curve remains unchanged. How does the market transition to its new equilibrium E2?

hints.text: Check what happens at the old price P* immediately after demand shifts right.
At old P*, Qd exceeds Qs (a temporary shortage), which bids price upward along the fixed supply curve until both P* and Q* are higher.

options_template.text: A temporary surplus emerges at P*, driving equilibrium price down and equilibrium quantity up.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): A rightward demand shift creates excess demand (a shortage) at the old price, not a surplus.

options_template.text: A temporary shortage emerges at P*, bidding price upward along the fixed supply curve so that both P* and Q* unambiguously rise.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rightward demand shift creates excess demand at P*, pushing price up and moving producers upward along S to a higher P* and higher Q*.

options_template.text: The supply curve automatically shifts rightward by the same distance so that P* stays constant while Q* rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Supply-Shift Fallacy): Higher demand induces a movement along the fixed supply curve, not a shift of supply.

options_template.text: Equilibrium price rises unambiguously, but equilibrium quantity is indeterminate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-vs-Dual Shock Confusion): Indeterminacy occurs with simultaneous dual shocks; a single demand shift moves both P* and Q* unambiguously.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Leftward Supply Shift
questions.prompt_template: When an avian flu outbreak reduces egg-laying flocks in the competitive egg market (holding demand fixed), how do the supply curve, equilibrium price, and equilibrium quantity change?

hints.text: Does avian flu affect producers' ability to supply eggs or consumers' underlying demand schedule?
The outbreak shifts supply leftward along a fixed downward-sloping demand curve, raising P* and lowering Q*.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward, causing equilibrium price P* to rise and equilibrium quantity Q* to fall via an upward movement along the fixed demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A leftward supply shift creates a shortage at the old price, pushing P* higher and reducing quantity demanded along D to a lower Q*.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward and demand shifts leftward simultaneously because higher egg prices reduce demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Shift Fallacy): Higher equilibrium price causes a movement along the fixed demand curve (lower Qd), not a shift of demand.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward, causing equilibrium price P* to fall and equilibrium quantity Q* to rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Direction Inversion): Losing flocks reduces output available at every price, shifting supply leftward rather than rightward.

options_template.text: Quantity supplied falls along a fixed supply curve with no shift of either curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): A biological production shock is a non-price supply determinant that shifts the entire supply curve.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Rightward Supply Shift
questions.prompt_template: In the market for utility-scale solar panels, improved wafer-slicing technology and cheaper polysilicon lower manufacturing costs at every output level (holding demand fixed). What happens to equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*?

hints.text: Lower production costs shift the supply curve outward (rightward) along a fixed demand curve.
At the old price, a temporary surplus pushes price downward, expanding quantity demanded along D.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward, raising P* and lowering Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Direction Inversion): Technological improvements and cheaper inputs lower marginal cost and shift supply rightward, not leftward.

options_template.text: Demand shifts rightward, raising both P* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-vs-Supply Confusion): Manufacturing technology and polysilicon prices are supply-side determinants, not demand shifters.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward, lowering P* and raising Q* via a downward movement along the fixed demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lower marginal costs shift supply rightward, creating a temporary surplus at the old price that lowers P* and increases Q*.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward, lowering both P* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Slope Violation): Moving down a downward-sloping demand curve as price falls increases Q*, rather than decreasing it.

questions.title: Dual Shock: Demand Increases and Supply Decreases
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market (such as Figure 3.3 or Table 3.1), demand shifts rightward (D increases) at the same time that supply shifts leftward (S decreases). Without knowing the relative magnitudes of the two shifts, what can we predict about the new equilibrium?

hints.text: Check each shift's individual effect on P* and on Q*.
Both D up and S down push P* upward, whereas D up pushes Q* up and S down pushes Q* down.

options_template.text: Equilibrium price P* is ambiguous, and equilibrium quantity Q* unambiguously rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Conflicting-Variable Swap): That outcome corresponds to D up and S up, not D up and S down.

options_template.text: Equilibrium price P* unambiguously falls, and equilibrium quantity Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Inversion): Both higher demand and lower supply push price upward, not downward.

options_template.text: Both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q* unambiguously rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored-Supply-Contraction Fallacy): While both shocks raise P*, the leftward supply shift pulls Q* down, making net Q* indeterminate.

options_template.text: Equilibrium price P* unambiguously rises, while equilibrium quantity Q* is ambiguous (indeterminate).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both shocks exert upward pressure on P*, but their opposing effects on Q* make the net change in Q* depend on which shift is larger.

questions.title: Dual Shock: Demand Increases and Supply Increases
questions.prompt_template: Suppose rising household incomes shift demand for electric bicycles rightward (D increases) while battery-manufacturing advances simultaneously shift supply rightward (S increases). Without knowing the shift sizes, what happens to P* and Q*?

hints.text: Evaluate the separate effects of D up and S up on price and quantity.
Both shifts expand Q*, whereas D up pushes P* up and S up pushes P* down.

Both D down and S up push P* downward, while they pull Q* in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q* remain unchanged because the two shifts cancel out.

questions.title: Reading a Binding Price Ceiling on a Market Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a supply-and-demand diagram (Figure 3.4, Panel A), a horizontal dashed line is drawn at Pc = $15 below the equilibrium price P* = $20. How is the resulting shortage measured on the graph?

hints.text: Follow the horizontal line at P = $15 across to where it hits the supply curve and where it hits the demand curve.
A shortage is a horizontal quantity gap measured along the Q-axis between Qs(Pc) and Qd(Pc).

options_template.text: As the vertical distance between P* = $20 and Pc = $15.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-vs-Horizontal Measurement): The vertical distance $20 - $15 is the price distortion in dollars, not the physical unit shortage.

options_template.text: As the horizontal distance between the origin (Q = 0) and Qs(15).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Traded-Quantity Confusion): The distance from 0 to Qs(15) is the quantity actually traded, not the shortage.

options_template.text: As the horizontal distance between Q* and Qs(15) only.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Gap Fallacy): Measuring only Q* - Qs(15) ignores the additional quantity demanded Qd(15) - Q* induced by the lower price.

options_template.text: As the horizontal distance between Qs(15) on the supply curve and Qd(15) on the demand curve, equal to Qd(15) - Qs(15).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Pc = $15, excess demand equals the full horizontal gap from Qs(15) to Qd(15).

questions.title: Reading a Binding Price Floor on a Market Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a supply-and-demand diagram (Figure 3.4, Panel B), a horizontal dashed line is drawn at Pf = $24 above the equilibrium price P* = $20. Which points on the graph identify actual quantity traded and the resulting surplus?

hints.text: At Pf = $24, check which curve lies farther to the left (the short side) and how wide the horizontal gap is between D and S.
At Pf > P*, Qd(Pf) < Qs(Pf), so buyers limit trades to Qd(Pf) and the surplus is Qs(Pf) - Qd(Pf).

options_template.text: Actual quantity traded is Qd(24) on the demand curve, and the surplus is the horizontal distance Qs(24) - Qd(24).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Above P*, buyers are the short side of the market (Q_traded = Qd), and the unsold surplus equals the horizontal gap from D to S at Pf = $24.

options_template.text: Actual quantity traded is Qs(24) on the supply curve, and the surplus is the horizontal distance Qs(24) - Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Side & Half-Gap Fallacy): Sellers cannot force buyers to purchase Qs(24), and the full surplus spans from Qd(24) to Qs(24).

options_template.text: Actual quantity traded remains Q* = 200, and the surplus is the vertical gap Pf - P* = $4.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-Gap & Fixed-Q Fallacy): A binding floor lowers quantity traded below Q* and generates a horizontal quantity surplus.

options_template.text: Actual quantity traded is Qd(24), and the horizontal distance Qs(24) - Qd(24) represents a shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Mismatch): Because Qs(24) > Qd(24), the gap represents excess supply (a surplus), not a shortage.

questions.title: Aggregating Individual Demand Schedules
questions.prompt_template: A local market consists of two consumer groups with weekly demand schedules q_d1 = 200 - 5P and q_d2 = 160 - 7P. What is the aggregate market quantity demanded (Q_d) when P = $15?

hints.text: Sum the two individual demand equations horizontally (add quantities at each price P) before or after substituting P = $15.

options_template.text: 90 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Averaging Fallacy): Market demand sums quantities across buyers rather than averaging them (180 / 2 = 90).

options_template.text: 180 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Summing horizontally gives Q_d = 360 - 12P, so at P = $15, Q_d = 360 - 12(15) = 360 - 180 = 180 units (check: 125 + 55 = 180).

options_template.text: 540 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Error Fallacy): Adding 12(15) instead of subtracting violates the Law of Demand (360 + 180 = 540).

options_template.text: 285 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Partial-Slope Summation): You summed the intercepts (360) but subtracted only the first group's slope term (360 - 5(15) = 285).

questions.title: Deriving Inverse Demand and Choke Price
questions.prompt_template: A direct linear demand schedule is given by Q_d = 500 - 20P. What are the choke price (vertical intercept) and visual slope of the plotted inverse demand curve?

hints.text: Solve Q_d = 500 - 20P for P in terms of Q_d.
Rearranging gives 20P = 500 - Q_d, so divide both terms on the right by 20.

options_template.text: Choke price = $25; visual slope = -0.05
options_template.feedback: Correct. Solving for P yields P = 500/20 - (1/20)Q_d = 25 - 0.05Q_d, giving a choke price of $25 and a visual slope of -0.05.

options_template.text: Choke price = $500; visual slope = -20
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted-Coefficient Fallacy): 500 is the horizontal Q-intercept and -20 is dQ_d/dP; you must solve for P to read the plotted curve.

options_template.text: Choke price = $25; visual slope = -20
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted-Slope Fallacy): While 500/20 = $25 is correct, the plotted slope dP/dQ_d is the reciprocal -1/20 = -0.05, not -20.

options_template.text: Choke price = $20; visual slope = -0.05
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Coefficient-Swap Fallacy): 20 is the price responsiveness coefficient b, whereas the choke price is a/b = 500/20 = $25.

questions.title: Computing Reservation Price and Quantity Supplied
questions.prompt_template: Regional coffee roasters have direct supply Q_s = -120 + 20P. What is their shutdown reservation price (vertical intercept of inverse supply), and how many units do they supply at P = $18?

hints.text: Set Q_s = 0 to find the reservation price, then plug P = 18 into the direct supply equation.

options_template.text: Reservation price = $6; Q_s(18) = 480 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-Sign Slip): You added 120 instead of subtracting it when evaluating Q_s(18) (120 + 360 = 480).

options_template.text: Reservation price = -$6; Q_s(18) = 240 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Intercept Error): Moving -120 to the other side of 0 = -120 + 20P gives +120 = 20P, so the reservation price is +$6.

options_template.text: Reservation price = $6; Q_s(18) = 240 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting Q_s = 0 gives 20P = 120 => P = $6; at P = $18, Q_s = -120 + 20(18) = -120 + 360 = 240 units.

options_template.text: Reservation price = $20; Q_s(18) = 360 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted-Intercept Error): 20 is the slope coefficient d, and omitting -120 overstates Q_s(18) as 20(18) = 360.

questions.title: Algebraic Equilibrium from Direct Schedules
questions.prompt_template: A competitive market is described by Q_d = 420 - 10P and Q_s = -60 + 20P. What are the market-clearing equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*?

hints.text: Set Q_d = Q_s and carefully collect the P terms on one side and constant terms on the other.
420 - 10P* = -60 + 20P* gives 480 = 30P*; then substitute P* back into either equation.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Sign Error): Subtracting 60 from 420 instead of adding gives 360 = 30P* => P = $12, where Q_s(12) = 180 != Q_d(12) = 300.

options_template.text: P* = $36, Q* = 60 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Subtraction Error): Subtracting slopes (20 - 10 = 10) and subtracting constants (420 - 60 = 360) gives P = $36, which fails to clear the market.
Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete-Substitution Error): 10(16) = 160 is only the subtracted term; Q* = 420 - 160 = 260 units.

questions.title: Solving Equilibrium from Inverse Demand and Supply
questions.prompt_template: Suppose inverse demand is P = 40 - 0.2Q_d and inverse supply is P = 4 + 0.1Q_s. What are the equilibrium quantity Q* and equilibrium price P*?

hints.text: Equate the two price expressions to solve for Q* first, then substitute Q* back to find P*.
40 - 0.2Q* = 4 + 0.1Q* simplifies to 36 = 0.3Q*.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Subtraction Error): Subtracting 0.2 - 0.1 = 0.1 instead of adding 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 yields Q = 360, which yields negative demand price.
Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal-Place Slip): Dividing 36 by 3 instead of 0.3 understates Q* by a factor of ten (12 instead of 120).
Diagnostic fallacy (Cross-Equation Substitution Error): You plugged Q* = 120 into a mixed formula 40 - 0.1(120) = $28 instead of 40 - 0.2(120) = $16.

questions.title: Quantifying Excess Supply Above Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: In a coffee bean market governed by Q_d = 500 - 15P and Q_s = -100 + 15P (where P* = $20 and Q* = 200), what is the exact market imbalance if the prevailing price is P = $26?

hints.text: Evaluate both Q_d(26) and Q_s(26), then take the difference between the larger and smaller quantity.
At P = $26, Q_d = 500 - 390 = 110 and Q_s = -100 + 390 = 290; since Q_s > Q_d, it is a surplus.

options_template.text: A surplus of 180 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $26, Q_s = -100 + 15(26) = 290 and Q_d = 500 - 15(26) = 110, creating a surplus of 290 - 110 = 180 units.

options_template.text: A shortage of 180 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Reversal): Because P = $26 > P* = $20, quantity supplied (290) exceeds quantity demanded (110), which is a surplus.

options_template.text: A surplus of 90 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Gap Fallacy): Subtracting Q* from Q_s (290 - 200 = 90) ignores the 90-unit drop in quantity demanded below Q*.

options_template.text: A surplus of 290 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Supply Confusion): 290 is total quantity supplied at $26; you must subtract the 110 units buyers still purchase.

questions.title: Quantifying Excess Demand Below Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Consider a market with Q_d = 320 - 8P and Q_s = -40 + 12P (where P* = $18 and Q* = 176). What is the exact market imbalance if the prevailing price is P = $12?

hints.text: Evaluate Q_d(12) and Q_s(12) separately and compare them.

options_template.text: A surplus of 120 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Reversal): Because P = $12 < P* = $18, quantity demanded (224) exceeds quantity supplied (104), creating a shortage.

options_template.text: A shortage of 48 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Gap Fallacy): Computing Q_d(12) - Q* = 224 - 176 = 48 omits the 72-unit contraction in quantity supplied below Q*.

options_template.text: A shortage of 120 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $12, Q_d = 320 - 8(12) = 224 and Q_s = -40 + 12(12) = 104, leaving a shortage of 224 - 104 = 120 units.

options_template.text: A shortage of 224 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Demand Confusion): 224 is total quantity demanded; subtracting the 104 units supplied gives the shortage of 120.

questions.title: Solving a Dual Shock Algebraically
questions.prompt_template: A campus bike-rental market initially has Q_d = 400 - 10P and Q_s = -80 + 20P (P* = $16, Q* = 240). Higher enrollment increases demand by 120 rentals at every price, while higher maintenance costs reduce supply by 30 rentals at every price. What is the new equilibrium (P**, Q**)?

hints.text: Update the constant intercepts of both direct equations before setting Q_d' = Q_s'.
Q_d' = 520 - 10P and Q_s' = -110 + 20P; set them equal to get 630 = 30P**.

options_template.text: P** = $21, Q** = 310 rentals
P** = $19, Q** = 330 rentals
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shift Sign Error): Adding 30 to supply (-50 + 20P) instead of subtracting 30 models a supply increase rather than a supply decrease.

options_template.text: P** = $20, Q** = 320 rentals
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted-Supply-Shock Error): Solving 520 - 10P = -80 + 20P accounts only for the demand shift and ignores the 30-unit supply contraction.

options_template.text: P** = $16, Q** = 330 rentals
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Fallacy): Adding the net horizontal shift (+120 - 30 = +90) directly to Q* assumes price stays frozen at $16.

questions.title: Equilibrium After a Per-Unit Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: A market has inverse demand P = 50 - 0.5Q_d and inverse supply P = 10 + 0.5Q_s (initial equilibrium Q* = 40, P* = $30). If the government levies a $6 per-unit excise tax on producers—shifting the inverse supply curve vertically upward by $6—what are the new equilibrium price P** and quantity Q**?

hints.text: Add $6 to the vertical intercept of the inverse supply curve, then equate the new inverse supply to inverse demand.
New inverse supply is P = 16 + 0.5Q_s'. Solve 50 - 0.5Q** = 16 + 0.5Q**.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Pass-Through / Zero-Quantity-Response Fallacy): Adding the entire $6 tax to P* ignores that higher prices reduce quantity demanded along D.
Diagnostic fallacy (Subsidy-vs-Tax Inversion): Subtracting $6 from inverse supply (P = 4 + 0.5Q) models a production subsidy rather than an excise tax.
Diagnostic fallacy (Unchanged-Price Fallacy): At Q** = 34, buyers are willing to pay P = 50 - 0.5(34) = $33, not the old $30 price.
Correct. Shifting inverse supply up by $6 gives P = 16 + 0.5Q_s'. Setting 50 - 0.5Q** = 16 + 0.5Q** yields Q** = 34 units and P** = 50 - 17 = $33.

questions.title: Quantity Traded and Shortage Under a Binding Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: A market is governed by Q_d = 360 - 6P and Q_s = -40 + 4P (where P* = $40 and Q* = 120). If the government imposes a price ceiling of P_c = $30, what are the actual quantity traded and the resulting market imbalance?

hints.text: Confirm P_c < P* (binding), evaluate Q_d(30) and Q_s(30), and apply the short-side rule.
Q_d(30) = 180 and Q_s(30) = 80; Q_traded = min(180, 80) and shortage = Q_d - Q_s.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 180 units; shortage of 100 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Side Fallacy): At P_c = $30, sellers only supply 80 units, so buyers cannot purchase 180 units.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 80 units; shortage of 100 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because P_c = $30 < P* = $40, the ceiling binds: Q_d(30) = 180 and Q_s(30) = 80, so Q_traded = 80 units and the shortage is 180 - 80 = 100 units.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 80 units; surplus of 100 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Mismatch): Because Q_d (180) exceeds Q_s (80), the 100-unit imbalance is a shortage, not a surplus.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 120 units; no shortage or surplus (non-binding)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Binding-Condition Error): A ceiling set below equilibrium ($30 < $40) is binding, not non-binding.

questions.title: Quantity Traded and Surplus Under a Binding Floor
questions.prompt_template: An agricultural commodity market has Q_d = 300 - 5P and Q_s = -60 + 10P (where P* = $24 and Q* = 180). If policymakers set a price floor of P_f = $30, what are the actual quantity traded with private buyers and the resulting imbalance?

hints.text: Check P_f > P* (binding), evaluate Q_d(30) and Q_s(30), and identify the short side.
Q_d(30) = 150 and Q_s(30) = 240; private trades equal min(150, 240) and surplus = Q_s - Q_d.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 240 units; surplus of 90 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Side Fallacy): Private buyers only purchase Q_d(30) = 150 units; sellers cannot force private consumers to buy all 240 units.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 150 units; shortage of 90 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Mismatch): Because Q_s (240) exceeds Q_d (150), the 90-unit gap is a surplus, not a shortage.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 150 units; surplus of 90 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because P_f = $30 > P* = $24, the floor binds: Q_d(30) = 150 and Q_s(30) = 240, so Q_traded = 150 units and the surplus is 240 - 150 = 90 units.

options_template.text: Q_traded = 180 units; surplus of 60 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Q / Half-Gap Error): Quantity traded falls from 180 to 150, and the surplus spans the full gap 240 - 150 = 90 rather than 240 - 180 = 60.

questions.title: Evaluating a Non-Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: Commuter transit passes have demand Q_d = 240 - 4P and supply Q_s = -60 + 6P. If the city enacts a price ceiling of P_c = $35 per pass, what are the resulting market price, quantity traded, and market imbalance?

hints.text: Always solve for P* first before plugging a regulated price into Q_d and Q_s!
Setting 240 - 4P* = -60 + 6P* gives P* = $30 and Q* = 120. Compare P_c = $35 against P* = $30.

options_template.text: Market price = $30, Q_traded = 120 passes, and imbalance = 0 (the ceiling is non-binding)
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equilibrium is P* = $30 and Q* = 120. Because the legal maximum P_c = $35 sits above $30, the ceiling is non-binding and the market clears at $30.

options_template.text: Market price = $35, Q_traded = 100 passes, and a surplus of 50 passes
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Blind-Substitution Fallacy): You plugged $35 into Q_d and Q_s as if a ceiling forced prices up to $35; a legal maximum above P* does not bind.

options_template.text: Market price = $35, Q_traded = 150 passes, and a shortage of 50 passes
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Blind-Substitution & Long-Side Fallacy): Not only is the $35 ceiling non-binding, but at $35 Q_s = 150 > Q_d = 100.

options_template.text: Market price = $35, Q_traded = 120 passes, and imbalance = 0
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-as-Target Fallacy): Sellers cannot charge $35 in equilibrium because a $35 price creates excess supply that pushes price back down to $30.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Bring It Home: Egg Price Spikes vs. Rent-Controlled Apartments
questions.prompt_template: Why did avian-flu shocks in the U.S. egg market produce temporary price spikes while grocery shelves remained stocked, whereas strict municipal rent-control caps produce persistent multi-year apartment waitlists?

hints.text: Compare how flexible prices versus legally capped prices ration scarce supply.
Flexible egg prices rise to clear the market and incentivize flock rebuilding; binding rent caps hold rents below P*, blocking price rationing.

options_template.text: Because eggs have an upward-sloping demand curve while apartments have a vertical supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Caricature Fallacy): Both eggs and apartments obey the Law of Demand; the key difference is price flexibility versus a binding legal cap.

options_template.text: Because flexible egg prices rose to ration scarce cartons and incentivize farmers to rebuild flocks, whereas binding rent ceilings froze rents below P* and turned scarcity into chronic shortages.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Flexible prices eliminate shortages by equilibrating Qd and Qs, whereas binding ceilings block price discovery and force non-price rationing.

options_template.text: Because egg producers are monopolies that arbitrarily raise prices, while landlords operate in a perfectly competitive market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Structure Misattribution): Egg farming is highly competitive; the price spike reflected a leftward supply shift, not monopoly price setting.

options_template.text: Because rent control shifts apartment demand leftward, eliminating all excess demand over time.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shift Confusion): A lower capped rent increases quantity demanded along D rather than shifting D leftward, worsening the shortage.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Unintended Consequences of Binding Municipal Rent Caps
questions.prompt_template: In high-cost coastal cities with binding rent-stabilization caps (P_c < P*), what non-price rationing outcomes and supply-side adjustments does the Chapter 3 model predict?

hints.text: When money price cannot rise to allocate scarce apartments, how do landlords respond on maintenance, conversions, and tenant selection?
Binding rent caps shrink rental supply (fewer new builds, condo conversions) and generate waitlists, declining maintenance, discrimination, or side payments.

options_template.text: Landlords accelerate new apartment construction and upgrade unit maintenance to attract tenants away from rivals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted-Incentive Fallacy): Lower capped returns discourage new construction and reduce the incentive to spend on maintenance when dozens of applicants wait for every unit.

options_template.text: Surplus vacant apartments accumulate because tenants refuse to pay the capped rent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): A binding ceiling creates excess demand (a shortage), not vacant surpluses.

options_template.text: Waitlists lengthen, landlords face weaker incentives to maintain units, some rentals convert to condominiums, and allocation shifts toward personal connections or black-market side payments.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When price cannot ration housing, scarcity manifests through queues, quality deterioration, reduced rental supply, and non-price screening.

options_template.text: All prospective tenants benefit equally because every applicant receives an apartment at the lower regulated rent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal-Beneficiary Fallacy): Incumbent tenants in controlled units pay lower rent, but excluded applicants face a shrunken supply (Q_s < Q*) and chronic shortages.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Policy Trade-Offs of Agricultural Commodity Price Supports
questions.prompt_template: Historically, when federal agricultural programs established binding price floors for dairy and grain above market-clearing equilibrium (P_f > P*), why did government agencies end up purchasing and storing millions of tons of surplus output?

hints.text: Compare private buyers' quantity demanded against farmers' quantity supplied at the elevated support price.
At P_f > P*, farmers expand Q_s while private consumers cut Q_d; someone must absorb the unsold gap Q_s - Q_d to defend the floor.

options_template.text: Because the above-equilibrium floor incentivized farmers to expand Q_s while discouraging private consumers (lower Q_d), leaving an unsold surplus (Q_s - Q_d) that agencies bought to maintain P_f.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without public surplus purchases, downward market pressure from excess supply would undermine the binding price floor.

options_template.text: Because the price floor created a severe food shortage, forcing the government to ration stockpiles to starving households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-Floor Inversion): A binding floor creates a surplus (excess supply), not a shortage.

options_template.text: Because private consumers refused to buy any agricultural products once the price rose above equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Demand Exaggeration): Private consumers still buy Q_d(P_f) > 0, just less than Q_s(P_f).

options_template.text: Because agricultural price floors shift the market demand curve rightward faster than farmers can harvest crops.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Shift Confusion): A price floor causes movements along fixed demand and supply curves rather than shifting demand rightward.

questions.topic: Minimum Wage as a Price Floor
questions.title: Evaluating Binding vs. Non-Binding Statutory Minimum Wages
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive entry-level labor market where the market-clearing wage is W*, how does a statutory minimum wage W_min affect employment and job-applicant queues depending on whether W_min > W* or W_min < W*?

hints.text: Treat the wage as the price of labor: employers represent labor demand and workers represent labor supply.
A minimum wage is a price floor—binding only when W_min > W* (creating a labor surplus of unfilled applicants) and non-binding when W_min < W*.

options_template.text: If W_min < W*, it is binding and creates a labor shortage; if W_min > W*, it is non-binding and has no effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Binding-Condition Inversion): A floor is binding above equilibrium (W_min > W*) and non-binding below equilibrium (W_min < W*).

options_template.text: If W_min > W*, both quantity of labor demanded by employers and quantity of labor supplied by workers increase, expanding total employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law-of-Demand Violation): A higher wage above W* reduces employers' quantity of labor demanded, which is the short side of the market.

options_template.text: Regardless of W*, any minimum wage law creates an equal-sized surplus of job openings that employers cannot fill.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage-Surplus Confusion): Unfilled job openings describe a labor shortage (excess demand), whereas a binding floor creates a surplus of job applicants.

options_template.text: If W_min < W*, the floor is non-binding and the market clears at W*; if W_min > W*, the floor binds, restricting employment to employers' lower quantity demanded and creating a surplus of unfilled job applicants.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A binding wage floor (W_min > W*) raises labor supplied above labor demanded, producing involuntary queuing for scarce openings.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing Airfare Jumps with Stagnant Passenger Volume
questions.prompt_template: During a peak summer travel season, industry analysts observe that average airline ticket prices jump decisively while total passenger volume remains nearly unchanged compared to the prior year. Which simultaneous shock combination best explains this empirical pattern?

hints.text: Look at Table 3.1: which dual shock unambiguously raises P* while leaving Q* roughly flat when the two shifts are comparable in size?
Higher vacation demand (D up) combined with higher jet-fuel costs or aircraft delays (S down) pushes P* sharply up while pulling Q* in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Demand shifted rightward (D up) and supply shifted rightward (S up) by similar amounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Dual-Shock Pair): D up and S up would cause passenger volume Q* to surge unambiguously while leaving price P* nearly unchanged.

options_template.text: Demand shifted rightward (summer travel rebound, D up) while supply shifted leftward (jet-fuel cost spike or aircraft delivery delays, S down) by comparable horizontal magnitudes.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both D up and S down drive airfares sharply higher, while their opposing impacts on Q* nearly offset each other.

options_template.text: Demand shifted leftward (D down) while supply shifted rightward (S up) by similar amounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted-Price Pair): D down and S up would cause airfares to fall sharply, not jump decisively.

options_template.text: A single rightward shift in demand with a completely unchanged supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Shock Mismatch): Along an upward-sloping supply curve, a pure rightward demand shift raises both P* and Q* noticeably.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting Falling Prices and Surging Installations in Solar Modules
questions.prompt_template: Over a decade, economists observe that the market price per watt of photovoltaic solar panels falls dramatically while global megawatt installations expand rapidly. Which supply-and-demand shift dominates this historical pattern?

hints.text: Ask which single-curve shift moves P* downward and Q* upward simultaneously.
Lower P* combined with higher Q* is the classic signature of a dominant rightward supply shift (such as wafer-slicing innovation and cheaper polysilicon).

options_template.text: A dominant rightward shift in demand caused by rising household electricity consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shock Mismatch): A dominant rightward demand shift would push both P* and Q* upward, contradicting falling panel prices.

options_template.text: A dominant leftward shift in demand caused by consumer skepticism of renewable energy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Direction Contradiction): A leftward demand shift lowers both P* and Q*, contradicting surging megawatt installations.

options_template.text: A dominant rightward shift in supply driven by manufacturing innovation and falling polysilicon input costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even if demand also grew over the decade, a much larger rightward supply shift explains why equilibrium price fell while equilibrium quantity expanded rapidly.

options_template.text: A binding government price ceiling that forced solar prices down while increasing installations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-Volume Contradiction): A binding price ceiling lowers quantity supplied and shrinks actual quantity traded rather than expanding installations.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Compounding Subscriber Losses in Streaming Markets
questions.prompt_template: A streaming platform raises its ad-free monthly fee from $15 to $20 in the same quarter that rival platforms launch cheaper ad-supported bundles and live sports packages. How does economic analysis separate the two causes of the platform's subscriber drop?

hints.text: Classify the platform's own price hike separately from rivals' lower-priced substitute bundles.
The platform's own fee increase is an upward movement along D; rivals' cheaper bundles are a substitute-price drop that shifts D leftward.

options_template.text: The platform's own fee hike causes an upward movement along its demand curve (lower Q_d), while rivals' cheaper bundles shift the platform's entire demand curve leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Separating own-price movements from substitute-driven demand shifts prevents management from misattributing competitive erosion solely to its own pricing.

options_template.text: Both the platform's fee hike and rivals' cheaper bundles cause movements along the same fixed demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Price Movement Fallacy): Changes in the prices of rival substitutes shift the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.

options_template.text: The platform's fee hike shifts its demand curve leftward, while rivals' cheaper bundles shift the platform's supply curve leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Misclassification Fallacy): Own price never shifts demand, and rival product launches affect demand for substitutes rather than production costs.

options_template.text: Rivals' cheaper bundles shift the platform's demand curve rightward because they expand overall interest in streaming.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Inversion): Lower prices for close substitutes draw subscribers away, shifting the primary platform's demand leftward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Future Price Expectations Move Today's Spot Market
questions.prompt_template: Suppose grain farmers with ample silo storage become convinced that wheat prices will spike sharply next quarter due to forecasted droughts abroad. How does this expectation affect the competitive wheat market today?

hints.text: If farmers can store grain and sell it for much more next quarter, will they sell more or less at today's price?
Holding back inventory today shifts current supply leftward, pushing today's equilibrium price upward immediately.

options_template.text: Current supply shifts rightward today because farmers rush to harvest and sell more wheat immediately, lowering today's price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expectation-Direction Inversion): Expecting higher future prices encourages storable-good producers to withhold current sales, not dump inventory today.

options_template.text: Nothing happens today because supply only shifts next quarter once the foreign drought actually begins.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Myopic-Supply Fallacy): Producer expectations are a current non-price supply shifter for storable goods, altering today's supply immediately.

options_template.text: Current supply stays fixed while buyers move downward along the demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unshifted-Supply Fallacy): Withholding inventory shifts the current supply curve leftward, raising today's price and moving buyers upward along D.

options_template.text: Farmers hold back storable inventory for next quarter, shifting current supply leftward and raising today's equilibrium price while reducing current sales volume.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expecting higher future prices raises the opportunity cost of selling today, shifting current S left, lifting P* today, and lowering current Q*.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Steeper Curves Amplify Equilibrium Price Swings
questions.prompt_template: According to the comparative-statics relationship dP*/d(alpha) = (dD/d(alpha)) / (b + d) for a positive demand shock, how do steeper (less price-responsive) demand and supply curves (smaller b and d) affect the market's response to a demand surge?

hints.text: Examine the denominator (b + d) when demand and supply are steeper (smaller b and d).
A smaller denominator (b + d) makes dP*/d(alpha) larger: equilibrium price must swing more sharply to clear the market.

options_template.text: Steeper curves dampen equilibrium price swings because neither buyers nor sellers react to price changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Volatility-Damping Inversion): Precisely because buyers and sellers adjust quantities very little per dollar, a much larger price jump is needed to close the shortage.

options_template.text: Steeper curves (smaller b + d) amplify equilibrium price swings for any given demand shock because large price increases are needed to induce quantity adjustments.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With smaller b and d in the denominator, a given horizontal demand shift produces a larger jump in P* and a smaller change in Q*.

options_template.text: Curve steepness has no effect on equilibrium price swings; only the horizontal size of the demand shift matters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Irrelevance Fallacy): Both the shift magnitude and the slopes (b + d) jointly determine the resulting price change.

options_template.text: Steeper curves reverse the direction of the price change, causing a positive demand shock to lower P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Reversal Fallacy): Because b > 0 and d > 0, the denominator (b + d) is always positive, so a positive demand shock always raises P*.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Excess Demand Sensitivity Under Price Controls
questions.title: Why Rent-Control Shortages Grow Larger Over the Long Run
questions.prompt_template: Using the excess-demand approximation Delta Q_shortage = (b + d) * (P* - P_c), why does a binding municipal rent ceiling of a fixed dollar discount (P* - P_c) typically generate a much larger apartment shortage in the long run than in the first few months?

hints.text: Compare how responsive landlords (d) and prospective tenants (b) are to rent levels over a decade versus over a single month.
Over the long run, both demand and supply become flatter (larger b and d), which magnifies (b + d)(P* - P_c).

options_template.text: Because demand and supply curves become steeper (smaller b + d) over time, which increases the shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Direction Error): Smaller (b + d) would shrink the shortage, and in fact long-run curves become flatter (more elastic), not steeper.

options_template.text: Because the equilibrium rent P* automatically falls down to P_c in the long run, eliminating the gap.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Self-Clearing Ceiling Fallacy): In growing cities, rising demand typically pushes P* further above P_c rather than pulling P* down.

options_template.text: Because both housing supply and housing demand become flatter (more price-responsive, larger b + d) in the long run as developers halt construction, owners convert units, and more renters seek capped apartments.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Larger long-run responsiveness (b + d) multiplies any given price distortion (P* - P_c), widening the chronic housing shortage.

options_template.text: Because price ceilings only apply to newly constructed buildings in the first year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Misattribution): Even under fixed coverage rules, the widening shortage is driven economically by higher long-run supply and demand responsiveness.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Emergency Price Caps After a Natural Disaster
questions.prompt_template: After a severe hurricane damages power grids and roads—shifting local generator demand rightward and local supply leftward so equilibrium rises from P1* to a much higher P2*—a state enforces an anti-price-gouging cap freezing legal prices at the pre-storm price P1*. What does the Chapter 3 model predict?

hints.text: Compare the legal cap P_c = P1* against the post-storm equilibrium price P2*.
Because P_c = P1* < P2*, the cap becomes a binding price ceiling that creates a shortage and weakens incentives for outside suppliers to rush in extra generators.

options_template.text: The cap becomes a binding price ceiling (P1* < P2*), creating a severe shortage at retail stores, encouraging hoarding/queues, and dulling the price signal for outside suppliers to ship in emergency stock.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Freezing price at the pre-storm equilibrium blocks price rationing during scarcity and removes the financial incentive to absorb high emergency-shipping costs.

options_template.text: The cap is non-binding because P1* was already the competitive equilibrium price before the hurricane.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stale-Equilibrium Fallacy): Whether a ceiling binds depends on the current post-shock equilibrium P2*, not the outdated pre-shock price P1*.

options_template.text: The cap shifts the post-storm supply curve rightward, ensuring every household receives a generator at P1*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Creation Fallacy): A binding price cap cannot expand supply; it restricts quantity supplied to Q_s(P1*) along the shifted post-storm supply curve.

options_template.text: The cap creates a large surplus of unsold generators because storm victims refuse to buy at P1*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): Holding price below P2* produces excess demand (a shortage), not a surplus.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Avoiding the Fallacy of Composition in Price Analysis
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a freeze in Brazil shifts the global coffee supply curve leftward, causing the retail price of roasted coffee to jump sharply while prices of most other goods and services remain stable. Why must macroeconomists keep this single-market price jump distinct from economy-wide inflation (Chapter 5)?

hints.text: Distinguish a relative price change in one market from a broad-based increase in the aggregate price index.
A coffee supply shock changes the relative price of one good, whereas inflation is a sustained rise in the unitless aggregate price level across a representative basket.

options_template.text: Because single-market supply shocks can never raise a product's nominal dollar price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal-Price Denial): A leftward supply shock definitely raises the nominal dollar price of coffee in that specific market.

options_template.text: Because macroeconomics ignores agricultural goods when calculating the Consumer Price Index.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Index-Exclusion Myth): Food and beverages are included in consumer price baskets, but one item's relative price jump does not equal broad inflation.

options_template.text: Because inflation only occurs when the government imposes binding price floors on every good in the economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Floor Inflation Fallacy): Economy-wide inflation is driven by aggregate macroeconomic forces, not universal price floors.

options_template.text: Because a coffee supply shock alters one product's relative price in a single market, whereas economy-wide inflation is a sustained rise in the aggregate price index across a representative basket of thousands of goods and services.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Keeping single-market nominal prices (Ch. 3) separate from the aggregate price level (Ch. 5) prevents confusing sector-specific relative scarcity with macroeconomic inflation.
